title: github/gh-aw — GitHub Agentic Workflows

GitHub Agentic Workflows (gh-aw) lets developers define AI-powered repository automation in Markdown with YAML frontmatter and run AI agents securely through GitHub Actions. The gh-aw GitHub CLI extension compiles each agentic workflow into a standard GitHub Actions workflow.
Use conventional GitHub Actions for deterministic builds, tests, linting, deployments, and reproducible scripts. Add an agentic workflow when a task needs reasoning or interpretation, such as issue triage, pull-request review, CI failure investigation, documentation maintenance, dependency analysis, or repository reporting. GitHub Agentic Workflows complements existing CI/CD; it does not replace it.
Built-in AI engines include GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini, and Pi. Agent jobs are read-only and sandboxed by default, and configured GitHub writes are normally applied through validated safe-outputs jobs with scoped permissions.
An agentic workflow has two parts: YAML frontmatter configures triggers, permissions, tools, and the AI engine; the Markdown body tells the AI agent what to accomplish. The gh aw compile command validates this source and generates the .lock.yml workflow that GitHub Actions executes. Learn how GitHub Agentic Workflows works.
Security and permissions
Security, permissions, and controlled writes are core design concerns. The supported agent-job path defaults to read-only GitHub access and sandboxed execution. Safe outputs buffer configured writes, validate them, and apply them in separate jobs with scoped permissions. These controls are configurable, so workflow authors must review permissions, tools, network access, and generated files before deployment. Learn how GitHub Agentic Workflows handles security and permissions.
Using agentic workflows in your repository requires careful attention to security considerations and careful human supervision, and even then things can still go wrong. Use it with caution, and at your own risk.
GitHub Agentic Workflows is supported by companion projects that provide additional security and integration capabilities:
Agent Workflow Firewall (AWF) - Network egress control for AI agents, providing domain-based access controls and activity logging for secure workflow execution
MCP Gateway - Routes Model Context Protocol (MCP) server calls through a unified HTTP gateway for centralized access management
gh-aw-actions - Shared library of custom GitHub Actions used by compiled workflows, providing functionality such as MCP server file management
Workshop
Tip
Ready to learn GitHub Agentic Workflows hands-on? The Factory Tour Workshop is a self-contained, step-by-step workshop repository designed to teach you how to build, run, and customize agentic workflows from scratch.

report.summary: GitHub's gh-aw lets developers define AI-powered repository automation in Markdown with YAML, compiled into GitHub Actions workflows.
report.background: GitHub Agentic Workflows (gh-aw) addresses the growing need to bring AI reasoning directly into software repositories. Traditional GitHub Actions are deterministic—ideal for builds, tests, and deployments—but struggle with tasks that require interpretation, such as issue triage, PR review, CI failure investigation, and dependency analysis. gh-aw fills this gap by treating an agentic workflow as a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter, which defines triggers, permissions, tools, and the AI engine. The gh-aw CLI extension compiles this source into a standard Actions workflow, allowing GitHub Actions' existing infrastructure to orchestrate AI agents. Security is a central design concern: agent jobs are read-only and sandboxed by default, with writes buffered through validated safe-outputs jobs. Companion projects add network egress control and MCP routing, while the overall system explicitly requires human supervision and careful permission review.
key_points: gh-aw compiles agentic workflows into standard GitHub Actions: Developers write automation in Markdown with YAML frontmatter, and the `gh aw compile` command validates and generates a lock file that GitHub Actions can execute. This bridges AI's reasoning capabilities with GitHub's familiar, deterministic CI/CD pipeline.

It supports multiple AI engines out of the box: GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini, and Pi are built-in choices. Users can select the engine best suited for their task and switch engines without rewriting the entire workflow, fostering flexibility and reducing vendor lock-in.

Security is built around read-only, sandboxed agent jobs: The default agent-job path grants read-only GitHub access and sandboxed execution. Configured writes are buffered through safe-outputs jobs with scoped permissions, meaning AI agents cannot directly modify repository content without validation and separate, restricted deployment steps.

Companion projects provide extra security and integration: Agent Workflow Firewall (AWF) enforces domain-based network egress controls, MCP Gateway unifies Model Context Protocol server calls, and gh-aw-actions supplies shared custom Actions. Together they give workflow authors more granular governance over AI agent behavior.

GitHub warns to use it with caution and at your own risk: Even with safety controls, agentic workflows can behave unexpectedly. Human supervision is strongly advised, and authors must carefully review permissions, tools, network access, and generated files before deployment.
report.impact: For the AI industry, gh-aw validates the shift from pure chatbots to embedded agents with clear boundaries—signaling a mature approach where AI reasoning plugs into existing DevOps practice rather than replacing it. Developers gain a standardized way to automate subjective, interpretation-heavy tasks like PR review and issue triage directly in their repositories, potentially reducing maintainer burnout and speeding up response times. Regular users will see faster issue resolutions and better-maintained dependencies. However, this also introduces new governance requirements: teams must now audit AI prompts, tool access, and network egress, and build review processes around agent outputs. The read-only, sandboxed defaults set a precedent for safe agent deployment, but the explicit risk warnings remind the industry that agentic automation requires disciplined supervision.
report.tools: If you want to try it, start with the `gh-aw` CLI extension itself (install via GitHub CLI) and walk through the Factory Tour Workshop repository. For hardened deployments, explore Agent Workflow Firewall (AWF) for network egress control, MCP Gateway for centralized Model Context Protocol management, and gh-aw-actions for shared custom Actions. These companion projects extend security and integration options for production use.
